opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I don't think it's a strict trade-off. The framing of "research versus product" is a bit misleading, at least for the kind of work we do on large language models.

When I think back to Llama, a lot of the most important research insights came directly from trying to ship something real. You think you understand a problem until you put a model in front of millions of people, and then you find out what actually matters: instruction following, robustness, safety behavior, how the model handles messy real-world inputs. Those aren't distractions from research. They're research questions, and often the hardest ones.

That said, there's a real tension, and you have to manage it deliberately. If everything is driven by the next quarter's product roadmap, you end up doing incremental work. You optimize benchmarks, you tune the last model a bit better, and you miss the bigger shifts. Some bets need a longer horizon: new architectures, reasoning, agents, better ways of using synthetic data and post-training at scale. Those things don't pay off in three months, and sometimes they fail completely.

So the way I'd think about it is in layers. You want a core team pushing the frontier model itself, with a lot of autonomy and a willingness to take risks. Then you want a tight loop between that team and the product side, so the signal from real usage flows back quickly into what you train next. And you want a smaller set of people working on genuinely exploratory stuff that may not touch product for a year or two.

The other thing I'd say is that open-sourcing changes the equation for Meta specifically. When you release models openly, the community becomes part of your research loop. People fine-tune them, break them, find failure modes, build things you never imagined. That gives you a kind of feedback you can't get internally, and it means frontier research and product impact aren't only measured by what ships inside Meta's apps.

Ultimately, the risk isn't spending too much on research or too much on product. It's having them disconnected. The best outcomes come when the people training the models feel the pain of the users, and the product people understand what's about to become possible.

r001.rationale: The response supports long-horizon research to pursue larger shifts, but does not cite avoiding future technological catch-up as a reason.

r002.rationale: It does not mention distilling capabilities from flagship models into smaller models.

r003.rationale: It says real-world usage can inform research questions and future training, but does not identify product use cases as a grounding for research evaluations.

fable-5.1.text:
That's the tension every big lab lives with, and honestly I don't think it's a tradeoff you solve once. It's something you have to keep rebalancing.

The way I'd frame it: the research is the product, on a long enough horizon. Llama didn't come out of a product team asking for a feature. It came out of a research group that was given room to train things that didn't have an obvious use yet. And then, almost overnight, that became the thing the whole company's AI strategy was built on. If we'd been purely optimizing for what the apps needed next quarter, we'd never have gotten there.

But you can't just hide in the lab either. What I found with Llama 2 and especially Llama 3 was that the product pressure actually made the models better. When you have billions of people who might touch this thing through WhatsApp or Instagram, you suddenly care a lot about safety, about latency, about multilingual, about things that an academic benchmark won't push you on. That feedback loop is real, and it's a competitive advantage Meta has that a pure research lab doesn't.

So the balance I'd argue for is this. Keep a core group with genuine freedom, a few years out, not tied to any roadmap. Protect them, and protect the compute they need, because that's where the next discontinuity comes from. Then build a very tight bridge from that group into the teams who ship, so that a result goes from a paper to a model to a product in months, not years. The failure mode isn't doing too much research or too much product. It's letting the two stop talking to each other.

And I'd add one thing about open source, because for Meta it ties this together. Releasing the models openly is both a research strategy and a product strategy. It gets you the community, it gets you the ecosystem, it lets the world find uses you'd never have planned for, and that in turn tells you what to build next. That's probably the most Meta-specific answer to your question: openness is how you make the frontier work pay off in the product, without having to choose.

r001.rationale: It argues for protected, long-horizon research as a source of future breakthroughs, but does not cite avoiding technological catch-up as a reason.

r002.rationale: It does not mention distilling capabilities from large flagship models into smaller models.

r003.rationale: It says product pressure surfaces concerns such as safety, latency, and multilingual performance, but does not identify product use cases as grounding for research evaluations.

astra-6.text:
I think you need both, and you need to protect the time horizons of both. If every research project has to improve a product next quarter, you’re going to miss ideas that take years to work. But if research never encounters real users, you can miss what actually matters.

The connection should be a feedback loop. Product teams bring concrete problems—where models fail, what people find useful—and research can turn those into deeper questions. At the same time, researchers need room to pursue things that don’t yet have an obvious product application.

So I wouldn’t measure everything with the same metric. For product work, you want reliability and usefulness today. For longer-term research, you want evidence that you’re advancing capabilities or understanding. The goal is to make those efforts reinforce each other without forcing them onto the same schedule.

r002.rationale: It does not describe distilling capabilities from flagship models into smaller models.

r003.rationale: It says product teams should bring concrete problems, including where models fail and what people find useful, to inform research questions.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you need both, and you need to protect the time horizons of both. If every research project has to improve a product next quarter, you’re going to miss opportunities that take longer to develop. But if research never meets real users, you lose a very valuable source of feedback.

So I would give frontier research room to pursue uncertain ideas, while making it easy for promising results to move into products. And that should work in both directions: product teams can show researchers where models are failing and which capabilities would actually matter. The balance isn’t a fixed percentage. It’s having that connection without making immediate product needs the only criterion for good research.
